course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 2
unit.description: Follow the Spanish, French, Dutch, and British colonies, the regions of British North America, Atlantic trade, slavery, and colonial society from 1607 to 1754.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: European Colonization
lesson.summary: How Spanish, French, Dutch, and English colonization differed in size, goals, labor, and relations with American Indians.
learningGoals: Explain how Spanish colonial institutions subjugated and incorporated Native peoples and Africans.
Explain how French and Dutch colonies relied on trade alliances with American Indians.
Explain why English colonization drew large numbers of migrants who settled on land taken from Native Americans.
lesson.bigIdea: Spain built institutions of conquest and conversion, France and the Netherlands built small trading colonies, and England built agricultural colonies filled with migrants who took Native land.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain how and why various European colonies developed and expanded. Compare what each empire wanted, who came, and how they treated Native peoples.

sections.title: Spanish colonies in the borderlands

blocks.text: Spain's colonial system rested on extracting wealth from the land. In what is now the United States, Spain founded St. Augustine in Florida in 1565, and in 1598 Juan de Oñate led settlers into New Mexico, where Santa Fe became the capital in 1610. Spanish officials built institutions that subjugated Native peoples, converted them to Christianity through missions, and incorporated them, along with enslaved and free Africans, into colonial society.

The Spanish ranked people by ancestry and demanded Native labor and tribute. Franciscan missionaries tried to replace Native religious practices. Spanish settlements in the borderlands were small and often served as military outposts to protect Spain's richer colonies farther south.

sections.takeaway: Spain used conquest, conversion, and forced labor to subordinate Native peoples inside a ranked colonial society.

sections.title: French and Dutch trading colonies

blocks.text: France founded Quebec in 1608, and the Dutch founded New Netherland, with its port of New Amsterdam, in the 1620s under the Dutch West India Company. Both colonies attracted relatively few Europeans. Their goal was the fur trade, not large farming settlements, so colonists relied on trade alliances and on marriage and family ties with American Indians to acquire furs and other products for export to Europe.

French traders and Jesuit missionaries traveled deep into the interior and allied with nations such as the Huron and Algonquin. The Dutch traded with the Iroquois at Fort Orange, near present-day Albany. Because these colonies needed Native partners, their relations with American Indians were more cooperative than in English colonies, although alliances also drew Native peoples into European rivalries.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: French and Dutch cooperation with American Indians was practical, not equal. Colonists wanted furs, and trade changed Native economies and sometimes led to conflict.

sections.takeaway: France and the Netherlands built small colonies that depended on trade alliances and family ties with Native peoples.

sections.title: English settlement colonies

blocks.text: England founded Jamestown in Virginia in 1607, Plymouth in 1620, and Massachusetts Bay in 1630. Unlike the Spanish, French, and Dutch, England attracted a comparatively large number of migrants, including many women and families, as well as other Europeans. They came seeking social mobility, economic prosperity, religious freedom, and better living conditions.

Private joint-stock companies, such as the Virginia Company, paid for early ventures. English colonists focused on agriculture, settled on land taken from Native Americans, and lived separately from them. This pattern of settlement caused more direct conflict over land than the trade-based French and Dutch colonies did.

sections.takeaway: England sent many families who farmed land taken from American Indians, which led to conflict over land.

connections.title: From empires to regions
connections.body: Topic 2.3 looks inside the British colonies to see how environment, religion, and labor shaped separate regions.
connections.transferQuestion: Why would colonies built on farming settlements and colonies built on the fur trade treat Native peoples differently?
connections.feedback: A strong answer notes that farming settlers needed land, which led to conflict, while fur traders needed Native partners, which encouraged alliances.
